subjective.question: ABC Company is considering a project in a diversified industry. The beta of the new industry is 1.8 with a debt-to-equity ratio of 40:60. The risk-free rate is 10% and the market premium is 7%. The debt-to-equity ratio for the new project is also 40:60 and the after-tax cost of debt is 8.2%. Calculate the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) of the project. (Tax rate 35%)
subjective.answer: Since the debt-to-equity ratio of the new project (40:60) is the same as that of the industry, the industry beta of 1.8 can be used directly as the equity beta — no un-gearing or re-gearing is required. Cost of equity (CAPM) = Rf + Beta x Market risk premium = 10% + 1.8 x 7% = 10% + 12.6% = 22.6% Weights: Debt = 40%, Equity = 60% WACC = (Weight of debt x After-tax cost of debt) + (Weight of equity x Cost of equity) WACC = (0.40 x 8.2%) + (0.60 x 22.6%) = 3.28% + 13.56% = 16.84% So the weighted average cost of capital of the project is 16.84%.

subjective.question: Consider the following data for Meezan Group of Industries: selling price per unit Rs. 25, variable cost per unit Rs. 10, fixed cost Rs. 80,000, initial investment Rs. 200,000 and output level 10,000 units. Calculate: (i) break-even units, (ii) contribution margin over sales ratio (C/S ratio), and (iii) break-even revenue.
subjective.answer: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost = Rs. 25 - Rs. 10 = Rs. 15 (i) Break-even units = Fixed cost / Contribution per unit = 80,000 / 15 = 5,333.33 units, i.e. approximately 5,333 units. (ii) C/S ratio = Contribution per unit / Selling price per unit = 15 / 25 = 0.60, i.e. 60%. (iii) Break-even revenue = Fixed cost / C/S ratio = 80,000 / 0.60 = Rs. 133,333.33.

subjective.question: Meezan Corporation is going to start a project in a new industry. Its current beta is 2, whereas the beta of the new industry is 1.7 with a debt-to-equity ratio of 40:60. The company wishes to maintain a debt-to-equity ratio of 40:60 for the new project. Is there any need to un-gear or re-gear the equity beta? Why or why not?
subjective.answer: No, there is no need to un-gear and re-gear the equity beta in this case. The purpose of un-gearing is to remove the effect of the source company's financial gearing from its beta, and re-gearing then applies the effect of the project's own gearing. Here the beta of the new industry (1.7) is measured at a debt-to-equity ratio of 40:60, and the company wishes to maintain exactly the same debt-to-equity ratio of 40:60 for the new project. Because the level of gearing is identical, the financial risk reflected in the industry beta is the same as the financial risk of the project, so the industry beta of 1.7 can be used directly as the project's equity beta in the CAPM. (The company's own current beta of 2 relates to its existing industry and is not relevant to the new project.)

subjective.question: The fixed cost of a proposed project is Rs. 45,000 per year, whereas the variable cost is Rs. 202,500. Sales are Rs. 270,000 and profit is Rs. 22,500. Calculate the degree of operating leverage (DOL) for the project and explain what it shows.
subjective.answer: Contribution = Sales - Variable cost = Rs. 270,000 - Rs. 202,500 = Rs. 67,500 Check: EBIT (profit) = Contribution - Fixed cost = 67,500 - 45,000 = Rs. 22,500 (as given). Degree of operating leverage (DOL) = Contribution / EBIT = 67,500 / 22,500 = 3.0 Interpretation: A DOL of 3 means that operating profit is three times as sensitive as sales — a 1% change in sales will bring approximately a 3% change in operating profit (EBIT), in the same direction. It shows a high degree of operating risk because of the relatively high fixed costs.

subjective.question: A company is considering investing in a new machine. The estimated useful life of the machine is 5 years. The net present value of the project at a discount rate of 12% is Rs. 425,000 and at 15% it is Rs. (80,000). Calculate the internal rate of return (IRR) of the project.
subjective.answer: The IRR is the discount rate at which the NPV of the project is zero. Using linear interpolation between 12% (NPV = +Rs. 425,000) and 15% (NPV = -Rs. 80,000): IRR = Lower rate + [NPV at lower rate / (NPV at lower rate - NPV at higher rate)] x Difference in rates IRR = 12% + [425,000 / (425,000 + 80,000)] x (15% - 12%) IRR = 12% + (425,000 / 505,000) x 3% = 12% + 2.52% = 14.52% So the internal rate of return of the project is approximately 14.52%.

subjective.question: A stock will pay dividends of Rs. 4.5, Rs. 3.5 and Rs. 2.5 in years 1, 2 and 3 respectively. After 3 years, dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 6% indefinitely. The required return on the stock is 12%. (a) Find the value of the stock after three years. (b) Find the current value of the stock.
subjective.answer: First find the terminal value at the end of year 3, when constant growth begins. Dividend in year 4 = D3 x (1 + g) = 2.5 x 1.06 = Rs. 2.65 (a) Value at the end of year 3, P3 = D4 / (r - g) = 2.65 / (0.12 - 0.06) = 2.65 / 0.06 = Rs. 44.17 (b) Current value P0 = Present value of D1, D2, D3 and P3, all discounted at 12%: P0 = 4.5/(1.12) + 3.5/(1.12)^2 + 2.5/(1.12)^3 + 44.17/(1.12)^3 P0 = 4.02 + 2.79 + 1.78 + 31.44 = Rs. 40.02 (approximately) So the current value of the stock is approximately Rs. 40.02.

subjective.question: The following information has been extracted from a company's books: net sales Rs. 500,000, EBIT Rs. 200,000, interest charges Rs. 50,000, tax Rs. 30,000 and total average assets Rs. 350,000. Find the total asset turnover and the net profit margin.
subjective.answer: Net income = EBIT - Interest - Tax = Rs. 200,000 - Rs. 50,000 - Rs. 30,000 = Rs. 120,000 Total asset turnover = Net sales / Total average assets = 500,000 / 350,000 = 1.43 times Net profit margin = Net income / Net sales x 100 = 120,000 / 500,000 x 100 = 24% So the company generates Rs. 1.43 of sales for every rupee invested in assets, and earns a net profit of 24% on its sales.

subjective.question: The market risk premium of a stock is 10.8%, the risk-free rate is 7.3% and the beta of the stock is 1.7. (a) Calculate the expected return of the stock and the expected market return. (b) If the beta is reduced from 1.7 to 1.2, how will it affect the expected return of the stock? Show calculations.
subjective.answer: (a) Expected return of the stock (CAPM) = Rf + Beta x Market risk premium = 7.3% + 1.7 x 10.8% = 7.3% + 18.36% = 25.66% Expected market return = Rf + Market risk premium = 7.3% + 10.8% = 18.10% (b) With beta reduced to 1.2: Expected return = 7.3% + 1.2 x 10.8% = 7.3% + 12.96% = 20.26% So reducing the beta from 1.7 to 1.2 decreases the expected return from 25.66% to 20.26%, a fall of 5.40 percentage points, because a lower beta means lower systematic risk and therefore a lower risk premium required by investors.

subjective.question: You have to purchase a car costing Rs. 500,000. Option 1: pay a down payment of Rs. 100,000 today and the rest of the money after 3 years. Option 2: pay the whole amount today and get a discount of Rs. 5,000. The interest rate is 8%. Which option is better? Show calculations.
subjective.answer: Compare the present value (cost in today's rupees) of both options at the 8% interest rate. Option 1: Pay Rs. 100,000 today and Rs. 400,000 after 3 years. PV = 100,000 + 400,000 / (1.08)^3 = 100,000 + 400,000 / 1.259712 = 100,000 + 317,532.90 = Rs. 417,532.90 Option 2: Pay the full amount today with a discount of Rs. 5,000. PV = 500,000 - 5,000 = Rs. 495,000 (paid today, so its present value is the same) Conclusion: Option 1 is better because its present value cost (Rs. 417,532.90) is much lower than Option 2 (Rs. 495,000). The benefit of deferring Rs. 400,000 for 3 years at 8% far exceeds the small discount of Rs. 5,000 offered for immediate payment.

subjective.question: A share has just paid a dividend per share of Rs. 5. The growth rate of dividends is 5% and the required rate of return is 10%. Calculate: (1) the current value of the stock, and (2) the value of the stock after one year.
subjective.answer: Using the Gordon growth model, P0 = D1 / (r - g), where D1 = D0 x (1 + g) = 5 x 1.05 = Rs. 5.25. 1. Current value of the stock, P0 = 5.25 / (0.10 - 0.05) = 5.25 / 0.05 = Rs. 105 2. Value after one year: D2 = D1 x (1 + g) = 5.25 x 1.05 = Rs. 5.5125 P1 = D2 / (r - g) = 5.5125 / 0.05 = Rs. 110.25 Note that the price itself grows at the same rate as the dividend (5%): 105 x 1.05 = 110.25.

subjective.question: A firm's fixed cost is Rs. 150,000, selling price is Rs. 50 per unit and variable cost is Rs. 30 per unit. Calculate the output level required to earn a target profit of Rs. 450,000.
subjective.answer: Target output = (Fixed cost + Target profit) / Contribution per unit Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost = Rs. 50 - Rs. 30 = Rs. 20 Target output = (150,000 + 450,000) / 20 = 600,000 / 20 = 30,000 units So the firm must produce and sell 30,000 units to earn a profit of Rs. 450,000. (Check: 30,000 x Rs. 20 = Rs. 600,000 contribution; minus fixed cost Rs. 150,000 = Rs. 450,000 profit.)

subjective.question: A project requires an initial investment of Rs. 90,000 and generates cash inflows of Rs. 40,000 per year for five years. The tax rate is 35% and the cost of capital is 10%. Calculate the annual depreciation by the straight-line method, the annual after-tax cash flow, and the net present value (NPV) of the project.
subjective.answer: Step 1: Annual depreciation (straight line) = Initial investment / Life = 90,000 / 5 = Rs. 18,000 per year. Step 2: Annual after-tax cash flow = Cash inflow x (1 - Tax rate) + Depreciation x Tax rate = 40,000 x (1 - 0.35) + 18,000 x 0.35 = 26,000 + 6,300 = Rs. 32,300 per year. (The second term is the depreciation tax shield: depreciation is a non-cash expense but it reduces taxable profit, saving tax of Rs. 6,300 every year.) Step 3: NPV = (32,300 x PVIFA 10%, 5 years) - 90,000 = (32,300 x 3.7908) - 90,000 = 122,442.41 - 90,000 = Rs. 32,442.41 The NPV is positive, so the project is acceptable.

subjective.question: An investor creates a portfolio by investing 40% in Stock A (expected return 12%, beta 1.1), 35% in Stock B (expected return 15%, beta 0.9) and 25% in Stock C (expected return 9%, beta 1.4). Calculate the expected return and the beta of the portfolio.
subjective.answer: Portfolio expected return = (0.40 x 12%) + (0.35 x 15%) + (0.25 x 9%) = 4.80% + 5.25% + 2.25% = 12.30% Portfolio beta = (0.40 x 1.1) + (0.35 x 0.9) + (0.25 x 1.4) = 0.44 + 0.315 + 0.35 = 1.105 So the portfolio's expected return is 12.30% and its beta is approximately 1.11. The portfolio beta and expected return are simply the weighted averages of the individual stocks' betas and expected returns, with weights equal to the proportion of funds invested in each stock.

subjective.question: What is meant by an aggressive and a defensive portfolio? How can the beta of a portfolio be used to classify it?
subjective.answer: The classification depends on the portfolio beta. A portfolio with a beta greater than 1 is called an aggressive portfolio because it is more volatile than the market: its returns move more than the market in the same direction, offering higher expected return but also higher risk. A portfolio with a beta less than 1 is called a defensive portfolio because it is less volatile than the market and its returns move less than the market, offering lower risk and lower expected return. A portfolio with a beta of exactly 1 moves in line with the market. For example, a portfolio with a beta of 1.4 is aggressive, whereas one with a beta of 0.7 is defensive.

subjective.question: The returns of a stock under different economic conditions are: 8% with probability 0.20, 12% with probability 0.40, 16% with probability 0.30 and 20% with probability 0.10. Calculate the expected return and the standard deviation of the stock's returns.
subjective.answer: Expected return E(R) = (0.20 x 8) + (0.40 x 12) + (0.30 x 16) + (0.10 x 20) = 1.6 + 4.8 + 4.8 + 2.0 = 13.2% Variance = Sum of Probability x (Return - Expected return)^2 = 0.20 x (8 - 13.2)^2 + 0.40 x (12 - 13.2)^2 + 0.30 x (16 - 13.2)^2 + 0.10 x (20 - 13.2)^2 = 0.20 x 27.04 + 0.40 x 1.44 + 0.30 x 7.84 + 0.10 x 46.24 = 5.408 + 0.576 + 2.352 + 4.624 = 12.96 Standard deviation = Square root of 12.96 = 3.6% So the expected return is 13.2% with a standard deviation of 3.6%, which measures the total risk of the stock.

subjective.question: Explain the process of un-gearing and re-gearing a beta, with the help of an example.
subjective.answer: Un-gearing removes the effect of the existing financial gearing from a geared beta to obtain the asset (ungeared) beta, which reflects only business risk: Beta(ungeared) = Beta(geared) / [1 + (1 - Tax rate) x D/E]. Re-gearing then applies the project's own gearing to the ungeared beta: Beta(regeared) = Beta(ungeared) x [1 + (1 - Tax rate) x D/E of the project]. Example: A geared beta of 1.8 is observed at D/E of 40:60 with a tax rate of 35%. Ungeared beta = 1.8 / [1 + (1 - 0.35) x (40/60)] = 1.8 / [1 + 0.65 x 0.667] = 1.8 / 1.4333 = 1.26 If the project is to be financed at D/E of 50:50, the regeared beta = 1.26 x [1 + 0.65 x (50/50)] = 1.26 x 1.65 = 2.07. This regeared beta is then used in the CAPM to find the project-specific cost of equity. Un-gearing and re-gearing are needed whenever the gearing of the project differs from the gearing of the company or industry whose beta is being used; if the gearing is the same, the observed beta can be used directly.

subjective.question: What is the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)? Explain the Security Market Line (SML) and how it is used to judge whether a security is undervalued or overvalued.
subjective.answer: The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) states that the expected return of a security is equal to the risk-free rate plus a risk premium based on the security's systematic risk (beta): E(R) = Rf + Beta x (Rm - Rf), where (Rm - Rf) is the market risk premium. Only systematic risk is rewarded, because unsystematic risk can be diversified away. The Security Market Line (SML) is the graphical representation of the CAPM: it plots expected return against beta for all securities. Securities lying on the SML are correctly priced (fairly valued); those above the SML are undervalued (they offer more return than required for their risk, so investors buy them) and those below the SML are overvalued. The slope of the SML is the market risk premium, and its intercept is the risk-free rate.

subjective.question: Define the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). Why is it an important concept in corporate finance?
subjective.answer: The weighted average cost of capital is the overall required rate of return of a firm, calculated as the weighted average of the costs of the different sources of finance (debt, preferred stock and equity), with weights based on their proportions (preferably market values) in the firm's capital structure: WACC = (Wd x Kd(1 - T)) + (Wp x Kp) + (We x Ke). The cost of debt is taken after tax because interest is a tax-deductible expense. WACC is important because it is the minimum rate of return a project must earn to satisfy all investors. It is used as the discount rate in NPV calculations and as the hurdle rate for accepting capital budgeting projects: a project is accepted if its return exceeds the WACC (or its NPV at the WACC is positive), because only then does it add value for the shareholders.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the Net Present Value (NPV) and Internal Rate of Return (IRR) methods of capital budgeting. Which method should be preferred when the two give conflicting results, and why?
subjective.answer: Net Present Value (NPV) is the present value of a project's future cash inflows minus the initial investment. A project is accepted if NPV is positive. Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is the discount rate at which the NPV becomes zero; a project is accepted if the IRR exceeds the cost of capital. Key differences: (1) NPV measures the absolute increase in shareholders' wealth in rupees, whereas IRR is a percentage rate. (2) NPV assumes reinvestment of cash flows at the cost of capital, while IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself, which can be unrealistic. (3) For mutually exclusive projects, NPV and IRR can give conflicting rankings because of differences in project scale and timing of cash flows; in such cases the NPV rule should be followed because it directly measures value creation. (4) Non-conventional cash flows can produce multiple IRRs, whereas NPV always gives a single, clear answer.

subjective.question: What is break-even analysis? Give its formulas, uses and limitations.
subjective.answer: Break-even analysis studies the relationship between costs, volume and profit (CVP analysis). The break-even point is the level of sales at which total revenue equals total cost, so the firm earns no profit and makes no loss. It is calculated as: Break-even units = Fixed cost / Contribution per unit, and Break-even revenue = Fixed cost / C-S ratio, where contribution per unit = selling price - variable cost per unit and the C/S ratio = contribution / sales. Its uses include: deciding the minimum sales needed to avoid losses, setting sales targets for desired profits (Target output = (Fixed cost + Target profit) / Contribution per unit), measuring the margin of safety, and evaluating the effect of changes in price, costs or volume on profitability. Its main limitations are that it assumes constant selling price and variable cost per unit, a single product (or constant sales mix), and that all units produced are sold.

subjective.question: Explain the degree of operating leverage (DOL), degree of financial leverage (DFL) and degree of combined leverage (DCL), with their formulas.
subjective.answer: Degree of operating leverage (DOL) = Contribution / EBIT. It measures the sensitivity of operating profit to changes in sales and arises because of fixed operating costs. A DOL of 3 means a 1% change in sales causes a 3% change in EBIT. Degree of financial leverage (DFL) = EBIT / (EBIT - Interest). It measures the sensitivity of earnings per share to changes in EBIT and arises because of fixed financial charges (interest and preference dividends). Degree of combined leverage (DCL) = DOL x DFL = Contribution / (EBIT - Interest). It measures the total sensitivity of EPS to changes in sales, combining both operating and financial risk. Higher leverage means higher potential returns but also higher risk for shareholders.

subjective.question: Differentiate between systematic and unsystematic risk. Why is only systematic risk rewarded in the Capital Asset Pricing Model?
subjective.answer: Systematic (market) risk is the risk that affects the whole market or economy, such as changes in interest rates, inflation, recession and political instability. It cannot be eliminated by diversification and is measured by beta; investors are compensated for bearing it through a risk premium. Unsystematic (diversifiable) risk is specific to a particular company or industry, such as a strike, loss of a major customer, or failure of a product. It can be reduced or eliminated by holding a well-diversified portfolio, so investors are not compensated for bearing it. Total risk = Systematic risk + Unsystematic risk. In a well-diversified portfolio, unsystematic risk is nearly eliminated and only systematic risk remains relevant, which is the basic assumption of the CAPM.

subjective.question: How is the value of a bond determined? Illustrate with an example and explain the relationship between bond price, coupon rate and yield to maturity.
subjective.answer: Bond value = Present value of coupon payments + Present value of face value = C x PVIFA(r, n) + F x PVIF(r, n), where C is the annual coupon, r is the yield to maturity (market rate), n is the years to maturity and F is the face value. Example: Face value Rs. 1,000, coupon rate 10% (annual coupon Rs. 100), 5 years to maturity, yield to maturity 12%. Bond value = 100 x PVIFA(12%, 5) + 1,000 x PVIF(12%, 5) = 100 x 3.6048 + 1,000 x 0.5674 = 360.48 + 567.43 = Rs. 927.90 Because the yield to maturity (12%) is higher than the coupon rate (10%), the bond sells at a discount to its face value. If the yield were equal to the coupon rate the bond would sell at par, and if the yield were lower than the coupon rate it would sell at a premium.

subjective.question: What is the payback period method? How is it calculated for uneven cash flows? State its advantages and disadvantages.
subjective.answer: The payback period is the time required for the cumulative cash inflows of a project to recover its initial cost. For uniform cash flows: Payback = Initial investment / Annual cash inflow. For uneven cash flows, the cumulative inflows are added year by year until the investment is recovered, with the fraction of the final year calculated proportionately. Example (uneven): A project costs Rs. 100,000 and yields Rs. 30,000, Rs. 40,000 and Rs. 50,000 in years 1-3. Cumulative inflow after year 2 = Rs. 70,000; a further Rs. 30,000 is needed from year 3, i.e. 30,000/50,000 = 0.6 of year 3. Payback period = 2.6 years. Advantages: it is simple to calculate and understand, and it favours projects that recover cash quickly, reducing risk and improving liquidity. Disadvantages: it ignores the time value of money (the discounted payback method corrects this) and ignores all cash flows received after the payback period, so it may reject profitable long-term projects.

subjective.question: Describe two approaches used to estimate the cost of equity, with examples.
subjective.answer: The cost of equity can be estimated in two main ways: 1. Dividend Growth Model: Ke = D1 / P0 + g, where D1 is the next expected dividend, P0 is the current market price and g is the constant growth rate of dividends. Example: if D0 = Rs. 5, g = 5%, P0 = Rs. 105 and hence D1 = Rs. 5.25, then Ke = 5.25/105 + 5% = 5% + 5% = 10%. 2. Capital Asset Pricing Model: Ke = Rf + Beta x (Rm - Rf). Example: if Rf = 10%, the market risk premium is 7% and beta is 1.8, then Ke = 10% + 1.8 x 7% = 22.6%. The CAPM approach is generally preferred when reliable beta estimates are available, because the dividend growth model requires a constant growth rate and a dividend-paying company, whereas CAPM directly links the required return to the systematic risk of the share.

subjective.question: Explain the concept of the time value of money. How are the future value and present value of a single amount calculated?
subjective.answer: Time value of money means that a rupee received today is worth more than a rupee received in the future, because today's rupee can be invested to earn a return, and because of inflation and risk. Two basic techniques are used: Compounding finds the future value of a present amount: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n. Example: Rs. 10,000 at 10% for 5 years gives FV = 10,000 x (1.10)^5 = Rs. 16,105.10. Discounting finds the present value of a future amount: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n. Example: Rs. 50,000 to be received after 4 years at 8% gives PV = 50,000 / (1.08)^4 = Rs. 36,751.49. These techniques are the foundation of capital budgeting, security valuation and loan decisions in corporate finance.

subjective.question: What is an annuity? Differentiate between an ordinary annuity and an annuity due, and give the formulas for the future value and present value of an ordinary annuity, with examples.
subjective.answer: An annuity is a series of equal payments made at equal intervals. In an ordinary annuity, payments are made at the end of each period; in an annuity due, payments are made at the beginning of each period, so every payment of an annuity due is discounted for one period less and its value is higher by a factor of (1 + r). Future value of an ordinary annuity = PMT x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r]. Example: Rs. 5,000 per year for 6 years at 9% gives FV = 5,000 x 7.5233 = Rs. 37,616.67. Present value of an ordinary annuity = PMT x [(1 - (1 + r)^-n) / r]. Example: Rs. 10,000 per year for 5 years at 10% gives PV = 10,000 x 3.7908 = Rs. 37,907.87. A perpetuity is an annuity that continues forever; its present value = PMT / r. For example, Rs. 2,000 per year forever at 8% is worth 2,000 / 0.08 = Rs. 25,000.

subjective.question: Explain the DuPont system of financial analysis. How does it decompose the return on equity?
subjective.answer: The DuPont system breaks the return on equity into three components to identify the sources of a firm's profitability: ROE = Net profit margin x Total asset turnover x Equity multiplier = (Net income / Sales) x (Sales / Total assets) x (Total assets / Equity). Example: With a net profit margin of 10%, asset turnover of 1.5 and an equity multiplier of 2, ROE = 10% x 1.5 x 2 = 30%. The system helps management and analysts see whether a high ROE comes from good profit margins (profitability), efficient use of assets (efficiency) or high financial leverage (which also increases risk). A firm can therefore improve its ROE by increasing margins, using its assets more efficiently, or employing more debt — although the last option raises financial risk.
